newsitem.title: UK: European bond markets jump after U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: European bond markets jump after U.S. data.

text.p: European debt markets jumped on Friday after a slightly stronger than expected rise in U.S. non-farm payrolls in January was off-set by a fall in hours worked and a rise in the unemployment rate.
Analysts said the data indicated strong growth in U.S. job creation without excessive inflationary pressure.
"The fall in weekly hours implies a slowing of the economy in the first quarter of this year," said Tom Hobson, director of technical analysis at Merrill Lynch in London.
Futures on French and German bonds hit new contract highs after the data and the British futures contract soared to an all-time high.
At 1447 GMT, March German Bund futures were quoted at 102.48, up from 102.19 before the data.
Gilt futures jumped to a high of 113-10 after the data, up from 112-12 before, and March notionnel futures pushed up to 131.26.
Payrolls rose 271,000 in January versus forecasts of a 237,000 rise. Average weekly hours fell to 34.1 from 34.8 in December and average hourly earnings rose only one cent to $12.06.

Analysts said the fall in the hours worked suggested the U.S. economy was further from full capacity than expected. "Some people may revise their first quarter GDP estimates down on (the fall in hours worked)," Hobson said.
"People believe the economy will eventually hit a bottleneck ... but when you have less hours worked it means that potential is not as strong," he said.
In the cash market, British gilts and U.S. Treasuries managed to take territory from Bunds after the data.
The 10-year gilt/Bund spread narrowed to 166 basis points from 170 before the data and the T-note/Bund spread closed in to 84 basis points from 87 before the data.

"Gilts are trading quite well after the data," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London. "Europe is following but not as much. That's been well overdue because the yield between Europe and the U.S. got to silly proportions and now Bonds are taking some of that back," he said.
Traders on the LIFFE floor said implied volatility of front month options on Bund futures fell to the lows of the year as the futures jumped.
Implied volatility measures the likelihood of significant movements in the underlying future. In a gradually rising market, volatility will tend to decline.
"It's a very frothy market. Volatility was crushed in the front month," said a trader at a French house at LIFFE.
"This is a very bullish figure for the market," said a trader at a British brokerage. "T-bonds liked it and the market is prepared to go with it."

Analysts said European debt markets' attention would now turn briefly to the weekend meeting of leaders from the Group of Seven industrial nations, although they expected little fall-out from the talks on Monday morning.
Continuing concerns over possible delays to European economic and monetary union would also return to dog the market, they said.
